passages.label: A
passages.text: The Oxford English Dictionary began collecting evidence in the nineteenth century. From 1857 until the initial edition was completed in 1928, editors and volunteer readers created millions of small paper slips. Many slips recorded a word with a dated example from a published source. Many also included a definition or an origin note. The archive therefore preserved more than a list, and it showed how a word appeared in use at a particular time, and this preliminary record allowed editors to compare examples, and they should not presume that today's sense existed in the past.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The slips helped editors determine which uses were supported by dated evidence. A discrepancy between two examples can be frustrating if the quotation is vague or has become partly incomprehensible. A grasp of regional complexities may be needed for a coherent account of how a word was borrowed. An explicit reference to a publication allows the evidence to be checked. Statistical information about frequency can help trace whether use changed radically, while a particular dated example still matters for showing where a word appeared. Volunteer readers copied passages from books, newspapers and other publications. Staff sorted the slips alphabetically. They could set dated examples beside one another and look for shifts in spelling or meaning, and the archive from the first edition contains more than five million slips.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Historical editors also examine word form and meaning together. Etymology uses regular sound correspondences and comparisons among related languages, and a modern resemblance is insufficient by itself. Two similar forms may have separate histories, while one form may divide into a number of meanings, and a word can be derived from another language and still change after adoption. Its spelling may shift, its pronunciation may adapt to a local dialect, and its meaning may narrow or widen, and this continuing interaction explains why an origin label is the beginning of a history rather than its complete explanation.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Oxford research shows that borrowing affected different layers of English at different times. Contact and settlement brought Scandinavian words into parts of the frequent core vocabulary. Later contact among French, Latin and English contributed heavily to high-frequency vocabulary and the wider lexicon. From 1500 onward, French and Latin also supplied much scientific and technical terminology, and other donor languages from Europe, Asia and beyond added words through trade, migration and intercontinental exchange, and these sources did not simply replace one another. They could coincide in the same period and become incorporated into different registers of English.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Printed records are evidence that an expression was in use, but an attested date can postdate its circulation in a dialect or in speech. An earlier text may precede an apparent equivalent by decades while leaving uncertain how the two forms are connected. For disambiguation, editors can collaborate with specialists who know a relevant terminology or historical setting. Sometimes a number of spellings coexist. The dictionary can incorporate new evidence when it arrives, because a preliminary account changes if older records alter the sequence.

R_H2.passageTitle: Restoring and Standardising Māori Place Names

passages.label: A
passages.text: In Aotearoa New Zealand, place names from different histories can coexist on maps. Names that refer to the same feature may not coincide in spelling or meaning, and a preliminary investigation can identify when each form was used and whether a community recognises a name from a local dialect. The New Zealand Geographic Board distinguishes formal approval from simply finding a name in a public record. Its process can incorporate records and community views before deciding whether to endorse a proposed official name.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A programme for recorded Māori names applies defined criteria, and a candidate must already appear in at least two publications or databases that the Board accepts as authoritative. There must be no other name for the place on an accepted map or in an accepted database, and mana whenua must not identify another Māori name for it. The Board must also consider public objection unlikely, and the programme changed in 2023 to prioritise recorded Māori names and to give mana whenua additional time to respond. Councils, mana whenua and the Board collaborate, although this approval route does not require a public consultation meeting for every name.

passages.label: C
passages.text: An explicit explanation of a proposed spelling helps readers determine why a discrepancy between maps matters, and some of the complexities of pronunciation may be incomprehensible to a reader without a grasp of the language. It can be frustrating when public records offer only a vague account of the original form, and a coherent decision needs advice from people who use the names and a way to explain whether a change would radically alter how people identify the place. The Board can check written forms with a qualified adviser before confirming the official spelling. Consultation with an appropriate language adviser can support disambiguation, especially when adding a macron changes pronunciation, and the spelling becomes an interface between records and signs, and people asked to collaborate may take a different stance on an older written form.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The standard treats dual and alternative names differently, and a dual name is one official string containing two parts, usually a Māori name followed by an English name. The slash joins the parts, and both are used together, and the order recognises first naming, although safety may justify an exception. Alternative names have equal standing but can be used separately or together, and the two forms are not necessarily translations or an exact equivalent. Some official names precede current policy because they arose through earlier legislation or Treaty settlements, while other names postdate those agreements.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The Board's 2023-24 report shows how these categories interact. It listed 22,790 official names and more than 630 current dual names. It also recorded 81 geographic features with alternative names. Another 27,560 names were recorded but not official, while 1,198 collected Māori and Moriori names preserved additional layers of occupation and memory. These totals describe a historical register rather than a simple translation table, and they also demonstrate that recording a name and granting it legal status are separate actions. Cooperation among communities, specialists and public bodies determines which evidence is strong enough for official action. The result is a naming system that can preserve more than one history while still giving users a clear form for navigation and public records.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A new technical term may enter French conversation before public bodies agree on a French equivalent. Under France’s 1994 language law, French has a defined role in areas such as education, employment and public services, and a separate commission works on terminology. Specialists may collaborate to prepare a preliminary definition and consider how an official expression can coexist with words already in use. The institutional process aims to clarify communication where an unclear choice could distort the meaning of an instruction.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A decree in 1996 created a coordinated process for developing specialist vocabulary as new concepts appeared in scientific, technical, economic and legal fields. Expert groups propose terms and definitions, which the Commission for the Enrichment of the French Language examines before the Académie française gives its opinion. Specialists can work with the Académie's Dictionary Service to refine the wording and definition. Publication in the Journal officiel gives the accepted terms a status that requires their use by state services in official texts and correspondence, regardless of whether the terms have yet become common in private usage.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A specialist needs a grasp of technical complexities to write a coherent definition, and an explicit explanation can help readers determine which French term matches a concept when there is a discrepancy between professional and everyday meanings. A vague definition can be frustrating or even incomprehensible to someone who needs to use it. Statistical evidence about the frequency of a word may indicate that use has changed radically, while speakers and specialists still have to decide whether a proposed term is suitable for an official setting. The Académie distinguishes lexicography, which records ordinary vocabulary, from terminology, which works on definitions of concepts in specialist domains.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Developing a term involves comparing possible word forms and testing the clarity of the definition, alongside examination of the expression's fit with French word formation. The Académie can support a well-formed option or reject a calque whose wording obscures the concept it is meant to name. Even after a recommendation is ready, its adoption remains uncertain because professional communities and the wider public influence which forms become established. The Académie has compared the choice to a wager because a formally approved expression must still prove intelligible and useful outside the process that selected it. Formal authority over government usage cannot determine how speakers will evaluate a term in every setting, and the choice depends partly on who needs the definition, because workers in a public service may require a specific distinction that is unnecessary in everyday conversation.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Cooperation with other French-speaking teams can reveal where speakers already use a different equivalent, and this interaction can lead specialists to incorporate a distinction into a definition for disambiguation. The approved term is published for the required settings, and a body may endorse such usage or enforce a rule within its legal scope. That is different from asking a term to displace everyday usage. Specialists may discourage a choice where it would create a dilution of meaning, while speakers outside the regulated context can continue to make their own choices.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the 1994 law do in the account given?
options: It makes the Commission responsible for recording all ordinary private speech.
It gives French a stated role in specified parts of public and working life.
It sets a grammar rule for replacing borrowed expressions in every conversation.
It specifies a fixed date when every newly published term must become common.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which sequence leads from a proposed term to a requirement for state documents?
options: The Académie makes a term binding, and only afterward do specialists give it a definition.
A term becomes binding when the public adopts it, before any official publication.
The Commission publishes each suggestion before seeking the Académie's opinion.
Experts propose the term, the Commission examines it, the Académie comments, and official publication establishes the requirement.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does publication establish even if a term has yet to become common among members of the public?
options: The accepted wording is required in the covered official texts and correspondence of state services.
The wording has become the normal choice in every kind of conversation.
The public must adopt it before any department can use it in a document.
The review panel’s requirements are lifted as soon as the wording is published.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How might a clear definition help when professional and everyday meanings differ?
options: It proves that the everyday meaning should replace the professional one.
It sets out how often each meaning has been used in the past.
It helps readers identify the wording that matches the specialist concept.
It makes both meanings identical in all contexts.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Suppose people begin saying a term far more often. Why could there still be a separate decision about its use where an institution has rules?
options: The more often a word occurs, the sooner it automatically becomes official.
That pattern leaves open whether the expression is appropriate for the required use.
The only purpose of the decision is to predict how quickly the new word will spread.
A rise in use means the original meaning can no longer be defined.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: When can the wording of a borrowed expression count against it?
options: When the term has been considered by more than one group.
When its spelling follows productive rules of French.
When it keeps a useful meaning separate for specialist users.
When the resulting words make the intended idea harder to identify.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What still has to happen outside the selection process for a formally approved expression to succeed?
options: Experts have to wait until the Commission repeats the publication vote.
Its use must become uniform in every legal and informal setting.
It has to prove clear and useful to the people who encounter it.
Dictionary specialists have to withdraw all older definitions first.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can specialists learn from other French-speaking teams before adding a distinction to a definition?
options: Other speakers may already use a different expression for the concept.
Private usage is necessarily the same in every French-speaking community.
Each team has the same authority to enforce a government rule.
Writers need to leave all existing meanings undefined.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which contrast best explains the limit of enforcement described near the end of the passage?
options: The rule becomes broader when more people use another term in private.
An institution may require the approved form within its remit, while speakers outside that context keep their own choices.
Being approved for official use also gives a term priority over every alternative at home.
Experts can choose what everyone must say, but state services may ignore the published choice.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What conclusion best reflects the whole account of agreeing on a new French term?
options: A clear definition and common private use automatically create a formal requirement for the term.
Institutions should wait until all professionals use a term before undertaking any work on its definition.
Publishing a term ensures general acceptance once its meaning has been stated clearly.
The process can improve precision and create an official requirement. Wider uptake still depends on those who use the language.
